A note from your professor: These eleven tutorial questions ask you to use the readings rather than repeat them: spot the symptoms of amnesia in a real person, link today’s findings back to Problem 2 and Problem 3A, explain a tricky result about memory for dates, and critically read the Soares and Storm article like a researcher. Each question below has: what it is really asking, a model answer, a figure, key points, a memory hook and where marks are lost.

Four honest notes. (1) I could not watch the video for B1 (I could only confirm its title, “Anterograde amnesia”), so I give you a checklist of the symptoms to look for and a model answer built on those criteria; tick off what you see. (2) B2 refers to Problem 2 (short-term and working memory). Those readings were not in this upload, so check the examples against your Problem 2 notes. (3) The Huppert and Piercy and Dewar et al. (2010) readings describe the direction of the results but give no exact numbers, so those bar heights are illustrative. (4) The figure for C3 was not attached, so I used Figure 1 of Soares and Storm (2018), which is the figure the question describes; values marked ≈ are read off that figure.

The big picture: Resource B is about patients whose memory recorder stopped saving new files (anterograde amnesia). The key idea is that memory is not one thing: these patients still hold a conversation (working memory), still know facts (semantic memory), and still learn skills and show priming (implicit memory). What they lose is the ability to bind an event to its context: the where and when. Resource C is about a healthy version of losing detail: people who take a photo remember the scene less well. Soares and Storm (2018) tested whether that is because we ‘hand the job’ to the camera (offloading) or because taking the photo pulls our attention away (disengagement).

Numbers marked ≈ are read off figures in your readings (approximate); bars labelled illustrative only show the idea.

Resource B · Amnesia

Question B1

Watch the video clip. Which symptoms qualify this man as suffering from anterograde amnesia?

🧭 What the question asks: Use the definition of anterograde amnesia as a checklist: show (a) that he cannot form new lasting episodic memories after a brain injury, and (b) that other abilities are spared, which is what makes it a selective memory disorder rather than general confusion or dementia.

✍️ Answer

Anterograde amnesia is a problem in encoding, storing or retrieving new information after brain damage, typically to the hippocampus and related medial temporal structures (Baddeley et al.). In its pure form it involves impaired episodic memory with preserved working memory, semantic memory, implicit learning and intelligence. The symptoms that qualify the man in the clip are:

  • He forgets new events and people within minutes: someone he has just met, or something he has just done, is gone once his attention moves on. This is the core sign: new episodes are not stored in long-term memory.
  • He repeats questions and stories, because he does not remember having asked or told them.
  • He cannot say what happened earlier the same day and may be disoriented about the date, the place or why he is there.
  • His short-term memory is intact: he can follow a sentence and hold a normal conversation, so the problem is not attention or working memory.
  • His general knowledge, language and intelligence are intact, and he can often talk about his life before the injury (retrograde memory is less affected, especially for older memories, in line with Ribot’s law).
  • Skills and habits can still be learned (implicit/procedural memory), like HM improving at mirror drawing without remembering having practised.
  • The problem began after a clear brain event (e.g., surgery, encephalitis, oxygen loss, Korsakoff’s syndrome), which marks the ‘anterograde’ direction: memory fails from that point forward.

Together, a severe, selective loss of new explicit memory with spared short-term memory, intelligence and implicit learning qualifies him as having anterograde amnesia.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Definition: can’t form new lasting episodic memories after brain damage
  • ▸Forgets within minutes, repeats himself, disoriented
  • ▸Spared: STM, language, intelligence, semantic memory, skills
  • ▸Older, pre-injury memories largely intact
  • ▸Onset after a specific brain event
The diagnosis rests on the contrast: new episodes are lost, but everything needed to use memory in the moment is still there.
🪝 Memory hook: His ‘record’ button is broken, but the ‘play’ button for old tapes and the live microphone still work.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Listing only ‘he forgets things’ without the spared abilities.
  • Confusing anterograde with retrograde amnesia.
  • Not naming the brain cause or the link to the hippocampus.
Question B2

Warrington and Weiskrantz (1970) showed a dissociation between explicit and implicit memory. We encountered dissociations before in Problem 2. In which context?

🧭 What the question asks: Recall where Problem 2 (short-term and working memory) used the same logic: one factor affects task X but not task Y, taken as evidence for separate memory systems.

✍️ Answer

In Problem 2 dissociations were used to argue that short-term and long-term memory are separate stores (the multi-store model), and that working memory has separate subsystems. The most likely contexts from your readings are:

  • Neuropsychological double dissociation between STM and LTM. Patient HM (after medial temporal lobe removal) had a normal digit span but could not form new long-term memories; patient KF (Shallice & Warrington, 1970) had a very poor digit span but could still learn new long-term information. Opposite patterns in two patients = a double dissociation, strong evidence for two separate systems.
  • The serial-position curve. A filled delay before recall removes the recency effect (items still in STM) but leaves the primacy effect (items transferred to LTM) intact, while slower presentation improves primacy but not recency (Glanzer & Cunitz, 1966). Each variable affects one part of the curve and not the other.
  • Working memory dual-task studies. A verbal secondary task (e.g., articulatory suppression) disrupts phonological-loop tasks but not visuospatial ones, and a spatial task disrupts the visuospatial sketchpad but not the loop. This dissociation is the basis for Baddeley’s separate components.

The link to Resource B: just as KF and HM showed that STM and LTM can fail independently, Warrington and Weiskrantz’s amnesic patients showed that explicit and implicit long-term memory can also come apart (poor recall and recognition, but normal fragmented-word completion, ≈ 45% in both groups).

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Dissociation = factor affects one task, not the other
  • ▸Problem 2: STM vs LTM (HM vs KF, double dissociation)
  • ▸Serial position: delay kills recency, not primacy
  • ▸Working memory: loop vs sketchpad in dual-task studies
  • ▸Problem 3: explicit vs implicit (Warrington & Weiskrantz)
Dissociations are the same argument in every chapter: if two abilities can break separately, they rely on different systems.
🪝 Memory hook: A light switch that kills the kitchen but not the living room tells you they run on different circuits.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Only saying ‘STM and LTM’ without an example or patient.
  • Describing a single dissociation as if it were double.
  • Not explaining why a dissociation is evidence for separate systems.
Question B3

Huppert and Piercy (1978a, 1978b) found that amnesic patients were more likely to say that items presented twice on day 1 had been presented on day 2; controls showed the opposite. How do these results show that binding item to context is a focal deficit in amnesia?

🧭 What the question asks: Explain the task, the two cues people can use to answer ‘which day?’ (familiarity vs context), and why the patients’ reversed pattern means they have the item but not its context.

✍️ Answer

The task. Participants saw pictures on day 1 (some shown twice) and on day 2 (shown once), then judged for each picture on which day it had been shown. There are two ways to answer. One is to recollect the context: to remember the episode in which the picture appeared (‘I saw that on the first day, in the morning session’). The other is to rely on familiarity: a general feeling of how strong the memory is. Familiarity is high for recent items, but also for items seen twice.

Controls had intact episodic memory, so they could link each picture to its day. Seeing a picture twice gave them a stronger item–context trace, so they were more accurate at assigning twice-shown pictures to day 1.

Amnesic patients still recognised the pictures, so their memory for the items was not gone. But they could not bind the item to its context (the day), so they had to fall back on familiarity. A picture seen twice on day 1 felt about as strong as, or stronger than, a picture seen once on day 2, and strong familiarity ‘feels recent’. So they misattributed it to day 2. As Baddeley et al. put it, without the link to context provided by episodic memory, they could not distinguish greater familiarity from two presentations from familiarity due to a recent experience.

Why this points to a binding deficit. The same manipulation (two presentations) helped controls but misled patients. The patients’ problem is therefore not a weak item memory in general, but a failure to link items to their time and place. The same pattern appears in source amnesia (Schacter et al., 1984: patients recall a trivia fact but not that they just learned it), in hippocampal lesions in rats (Winocur & Mills, 1970), and in Horner et al. (2012), where hippocampal volume predicted memory for context but not for items. The hippocampus acts as the ‘mnemonic glue’ that binds items to context.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

ControlsAmnesic patients
Recognise the picture?YesYes (item memory present)
Cue used for ‘which day?’Context (recollection)Familiarity only
Effect of seeing it twice on day 1Stronger context link → more ‘day 1’Feels stronger = recent → ‘day 2’
ConclusionBinding intactItem–context binding fails

📌 Key points

  • ▸Two cues for timing: context vs familiarity
  • ▸Controls: repetition helps → more accurate ‘day 1’
  • ▸Patients: repetition misleads → ‘day 2’
  • ▸Items remembered, context lost → binding deficit
  • ▸Same idea: source amnesia; hippocampus = ‘glue’
A reversal is more informative than a simple impairment: the same repetition helps one group and misleads the other, so the two groups must be using different information.
🪝 Memory hook: You know a song is familiar, but not whether you heard it this morning or ten times last year: familiarity has no time stamp; context does.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Saying patients ‘forgot the pictures’: they recognised them.
  • Not explaining why repetition makes the patients choose day 2.
  • Missing the link to the hippocampus and source amnesia.
Question B4

In developmental amnesia, ‘remembering’ and ‘knowing’ are discussed. We encountered both notions in the readings for Problem 3A. In which context?

🧭 What the question asks: First show you understand the distinction (recollection vs familiarity without recollection) and how it was used with Jon; then find where Problem 3A used the same remember/know judgements: in the study of childhood amnesia.

✍️ Answer

Remembering is recollecting an episode, mentally travelling back in time to re-experience it; knowing is recognising that something was encountered before, without re-experiencing the episode. In developmental amnesia, Jon (hippocampal damage at birth) had poor recall but near-normal recognition. When asked to classify his recognition as ‘remember’ or ‘know’, he used both categories about as often as controls, but his ‘remember’ responses lacked the brain signature of recollection (Düzel et al., 2001). This fits the proposal that recollection depends on the hippocampus and familiarity on the perirhinal cortex (Aggleton & Brown, 1999).

In Problem 3A the same distinction appeared in the context of childhood amnesia (Robinson-Riegler). Multhaup, Johnson and Tetrick (2005) asked adults to judge their memories of events from early childhood as ones they truly remember (re-experience) or only know about (e.g., from family stories or photos). Memories from the earliest years were mostly ‘known’; the proportion of ‘remembered’ memories rose with age, with childhood amnesia waning at about 4.7 years.

More broadly, 3A also linked the two notions to the episodic vs semantic parts of autobiographical memory: an autobiographical memory is re-experienced (remembering), whereas an autobiographical fact is simply known (knowing), and repeated episodes can turn from the first into the second.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Remember = re-experience; know = familiarity only
  • ▸Jon: recognition OK, recollection lacking (Düzel et al., 2001)
  • ▸3A: Multhaup et al. (2005), childhood amnesia
  • ▸Early memories ‘known’ → ‘remembered’ from ~4.7 years
  • ▸Also: autobiographical memory vs autobiographical fact
Both readings use remember/know to separate re-living from knowing about the past, and both link re-living to a system that is not yet (childhood) or no longer (Jon) fully working.
🪝 Memory hook: You know you went to your 2nd birthday party because of the photo; you remember your 10th because you can still taste the cake.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Defining the terms but not naming the 3A study.
  • Mixing up which one depends on the hippocampus.
  • Forgetting that Jon’s ‘know’ responses were preserved.
Question B5

People with memory problems undergo a variety of tests during neuropsychological screening. How might this lead to an underestimate of the recall abilities of anterograde amnesiacs?

🧭 What the question asks: Link testing practice to consolidation and interference: tests given in the delay between learning and recall act as interfering material, and amnesic patients are especially vulnerable to interference early in consolidation.

✍️ Answer

In a typical screening session a patient learns something (e.g., a story or word list), then completes several other tests (digit span, naming, fluency, figure copying) before being asked to recall the first material. For a healthy person this filled delay matters little. For amnesic patients it matters a great deal.

New memories are initially fragile and need consolidation to become stable, a process that depends on the hippocampus and is most vulnerable in its early stages (Müller & Pilzecker, 1900). Della Sala’s group showed that amnesic patients are especially sensitive to interference during this window. In Dewar, Cowan and Della Sala (2010), four densely amnesic patients and six controls tried to recall a story after one hour. When the hour was spent resting in a quiet, dark room, the patients performed almost as well as controls. When the hour was filled with the sort of cognitive tasks that would normally constitute patient assessment, the patients remembered virtually nothing. Dewar et al. (2009) found that interference early after learning was most harmful for patients with mild cognitive impairment.

So a test battery creates the very interference that wipes out the patients’ recently learned material. Their low recall scores then reflect the testing situation as much as their true capacity: the battery underestimates what they could recall under interference-free conditions. Additional factors can add to this: fatigue and reduced motivation over a long session, and proactive interference when several similar tests (e.g., word lists) follow each other.

The practical implication: clinicians should build in interference-free rest after learning, and rehabilitation can use quiet rest to improve retention.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Screening = many tests in a row
  • ▸Tests in the delay = interfering material
  • ▸Amnesics: consolidation fragile, very sensitive to early interference
  • ▸Quiet dark room: patients almost like controls (Dewar et al., 2010)
  • ▸So scores underestimate true recall ability
The measurement changes what is measured: the battery itself causes forgetting in the patients it is meant to assess.
🪝 Memory hook: It’s like testing whether wet cement holds a footprint while people keep walking over it.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Only saying ‘patients get tired’.
  • Not naming consolidation and interference.
  • Missing the Della Sala / Dewar evidence.
Forget in a flash: A further investigation of the photo-taking-impairment effect

Resource C · Soares & Storm (2018)

Question C1

Use the reading instructions to review the Soares and Storm (2018) article: IVs, manipulation, DV, results, effect sizes, significance, causation and generalisation.

🧭 What the question asks: Read the article like a researcher. Answer each of the seven sub-questions briefly and precisely, with the numbers from the paper.

✍️ Answer

Independent variable(s). One IV per experiment: photo-taking condition, with three levels. Experiment 1: Observe, Camera (photo saved in the photo album), Snapchat (photo sent and not saved). Experiment 2: Observe, Camera, Delete (photo taken and immediately deleted, followed by 15 s of viewing).

Manipulated? Within or between? Yes, it was manipulated by the researchers, within participants: every participant did all three conditions, each on a block of five paintings. A Latin square counterbalanced which paintings went with which condition and the order of the conditions; in Experiment 2 participants were randomly assigned to the counterbalancing orders.

Dependent variable and measurement. Memory for visual details of the paintings: a 30-item multiple-choice test (two questions per painting, four options each, chance = .25), given after a 10-minute Tetris filler task, scored as proportion correct by an experimenter blind to condition.

Highest and lowest; effect sizes. Experiment 1: Observe highest (≈ .58), Camera (≈ .45), Snapchat lowest (≈ .36). Camera < Observe, d = 0.70; Snapchat < Observe, d = 1.21; Snapchat < Camera, d = 0.48; overall ηp² = .27. Experiment 2: Observe highest (≈ .56), Camera (≈ .49) and Delete (≈ .48) lowest and not different from each other. Camera < Observe, d = 0.58; Delete < Observe, d = 0.61; overall ηp² = .08. These are medium to large effects.

Statistically significant? Yes. Experiment 1: F(2, 82) = 15.35, p < .001, and all three planned comparisons (p = .003, p < .001, p = .031). Experiment 2: F(2, 100) = 4.26, p = .017; Camera vs Observe p = .026, Delete vs Observe p = .005; Camera vs Delete not significant, t(50) = 0.25, p = .80.

Conditions of causation. (1) Covariation: memory differs across conditions. (2) Temporal order: the condition was manipulated before memory was measured. (3) Alternative explanations: the within-subjects design controls individual differences; counterbalancing controls painting difficulty and order; scoring was blind; Experiment 2 equalised viewing time and made ‘no access’ believable. So the authors make it plausible that the photo-taking procedure causes the impairment. What is not settled is which part of the procedure (handling the phone, the switch between tasks, a metacognitive illusion). In Experiment 1, less viewing time in the Snapchat condition was a confound, which Experiment 2 fixed.

Generalisation. The authors generalise to people photographing experiences in daily life (‘for a truly memorable experience… it might sometimes be best to put the camera away’). This is only partly convincing. Support: the effect replicates Henkel’s (2014) museum field study. Limits: small samples of UCSC undergraduates doing it for course credit; paintings on a screen in a lab; instructed rather than self-chosen photos; a short 10-minute delay; a test only of visual details; photos were never reviewed. Volitional photography can even improve visual memory (Barasch et al., 2017).

🖼️ The answer in one picture

Experiment 1 (n = 42)Experiment 2 (n = 51)
IV levelsObserve, Camera, SnapchatObserve, Camera, Delete
DesignWithin; Latin squareWithin; Latin square; random assignment to orders
Viewing time15 s including photo15 s after the photo
Means (≈).58 / .45 / .36.56 / .49 / .48
Overall testF(2,82) = 15.35, p < .001, ηp² = .27F(2,100) = 4.26, p = .017, ηp² = .08
Key dCam–Obs 0.70; Snap–Obs 1.21; Snap–Cam 0.48Cam–Obs 0.58; Del–Obs 0.61; Cam = Del

📌 Key points

  • ▸IV: photo condition (3 levels), manipulated within subjects
  • ▸DV: proportion correct on 30 MC visual-detail items
  • ▸Observe best; Snapchat (Exp 1) / Camera = Delete (Exp 2) worst
  • ▸All key effects significant, d ≈ 0.5–1.2
  • ▸Causal claim plausible; mechanism and generalisation limited
The study shows that photo-taking impairs memory under controlled conditions; it does not yet show why, or how far it generalises.
🪝 Memory hook: IV-DV-Result-Stats-Cause-Who: ‘I Don’t Really Study Causes Wrongly’.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Calling the design between-subjects.
  • Giving means without effect sizes or stats.
  • Accepting the generalisation without naming sample, setting and instructed photos.
Question C2

Provide alternative examples of transactive memories between people, and between people and devices.

🧭 What the question asks: Give your own examples (not only Wegner’s couples) that show the core idea: you remember who or what knows the information, and rely on it.

✍️ Answer

Transactive memory (Wegner, 1987) is a shared memory system in which people store information in each other, or in objects, and remember who or what knows what.

Between people:

  • In a family, one parent keeps track of school dates and the other of dentist appointments; each knows to ask the other.
  • In a work team, you don’t memorise the payroll rules because you know Anna does, and IT questions go to Tom.
  • Friends on holiday: one remembers the name of the restaurant, the other the route back to the hotel.
  • Siblings who each hold different parts of family history and together reconstruct a story.

Between people and devices:

  • You no longer know phone numbers by heart, but you know your contacts app has them.
  • Appointments live in a calendar app, so you stop rehearsing them (and forget them if the phone dies).
  • For facts, you remember where to find them (a search engine) rather than the fact itself (Sparrow, Liu & Wegner, 2011).
  • Navigation apps hold the route, so you learn less of the city layout.

In each case the benefit is freed-up capacity (Storm & Stone, 2015); the cost is that the information is hard to recall when the partner or device is unavailable.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Remember who/what knows, not the content
  • ▸People: family, work team, friends, siblings
  • ▸Devices: contacts, calendar, search engine, navigation
  • ▸Benefit: frees resources; cost: dependence
A good example always has two parts: the information is stored elsewhere, and you know where.
🪝 Memory hook: Your brain keeps the index; the phone keeps the book.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Examples of simply forgetting, without relying on a partner.
  • Only repeating Wegner’s couples.
  • No benefit/cost.
Question C3

What would Figure 1 of Soares and Storm (2018) look like if the offloading account of the photo-taking-impairment effect were correct?

🧭 What the question asks: Derive a prediction from the offloading hypothesis and draw it: which bars go up, which stay down?

✍️ Answer

The offloading hypothesis (Henkel, 2014) says that people remember photographed objects less because they count on the camera to remember for them. It therefore predicts impairment only when people expect to be able to use the photo later.

  • Observe: highest, as in the real data.
  • Camera (photo saved): lower than Observe, because people offload onto the saved photo. This matches the real data.
  • Snapchat (Exp 1) and Delete (Exp 2): the photo cannot be used later, so there is nothing to offload to. Memory should be about as good as Observe, and at least clearly better than Camera.

So the third bar in each experiment would rise back up to (or near) the Observe bar, leaving Camera as the only low bar. In the real figure the opposite happened: the Snapchat bar was even lower than Camera (≈ .36 vs .45) and Delete equalled Camera (≈ .48 vs .49). This pattern contradicts the offloading account and supports attentional disengagement.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Offloading: impairment only if the photo is available later
  • ▸Prediction: Observe ≈ Snapchat/Delete > Camera
  • ▸Actual: Snapchat/Delete ≤ Camera
  • ▸So offloading is not supported
The decisive bar is the third one: it is the condition where offloading is impossible.
🪝 Memory hook: If you know the notebook will be burned, you don’t rely on it; so memory should be back to normal. It wasn’t.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Drawing all bars equal.
  • Predicting that Camera would be as good as Observe.
  • Not comparing the prediction with the real figure.
Question C4

Which of the two experiments has the strongest design? Why?

🧭 What the question asks: Compare the experiments on internal validity: which one rules out more alternative explanations? Name the specific confounds that Experiment 2 fixed.

✍️ Answer

Experiment 2 has the stronger design. Both experiments are within-subjects and counterbalanced with a Latin square, but Experiment 2 removes the two weaknesses the authors themselves identified in Experiment 1:

  • Viewing time. In Experiment 1 the photo had to be taken within the 15 s, so photo conditions had less looking time, and Snapchat probably took longer to use than Camera. In Experiment 2 the 15 s of viewing started only after the photo was taken (and deleted), so photo conditions had equal or even more total exposure. The impairment still appeared, which rules out ‘less looking time’.
  • Believability of the manipulation. Participants may not have fully believed that Snapchat photos would be unavailable. In the Delete condition participants deleted the photo themselves, so they knew it was gone.
  • Sample size. Experiment 2 used a power analysis based on Experiment 1 (n ≥ 49 for 90% power), with n = 51 and random assignment to counterbalancing orders.

Experiment 1 did produce a larger effect (ηp² = .27 vs .08), but a larger effect in a design with confounds is less convincing than a smaller effect in a cleaner design. One remaining limitation of Experiment 2 is that only 31 of 51 participants completed the survey, but this does not affect the main result.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Both: within-subjects, Latin square
  • ▸Exp 2 equalised (even increased) viewing time
  • ▸Exp 2 made ‘no access’ certain (Delete)
  • ▸Exp 2 power analysis: n ≥ 49 for 90%
  • ▸Stronger design ≠ larger effect
The strongest design is the one that leaves the fewest alternative explanations, not the one with the biggest effect.
🪝 Memory hook: Experiment 1 asked the question; Experiment 2 closed the loopholes.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Choosing Experiment 1 because the effect was bigger.
  • Not naming the time confound.
  • Forgetting the power analysis.
Question C5

Participants who took and deleted a photo, then observed the painting for as long as Observe participants, still remembered it less. How do the authors explain this? Could it also be a task-switching effect?

🧭 What the question asks: Give the authors’ explanation(s) of this ‘prospective’ impairment, then evaluate a task-switching account and say how you could test it.

✍️ Answer

The authors’ explanation. The finding shows that photo-taking does not only disrupt encoding while the photo is taken, but prospectively impairs encoding after the camera is put down. The authors favour attentional disengagement that continues after the photo, and offer two speculative mechanisms: (1) a metacognitive illusion: taking the photo gives a feeling of encoding fluency, so participants think they have already encoded the painting and invest less effort in the following 15 s (Bjork, Dunlosky & Kornell, 2013; Koriat, 1993); and (2) automatic (implicit) offloading: through years of experience, photographing has become linked with ‘this is stored elsewhere’, so people encode less even when they consciously know the photo is deleted. They also note that any secondary task might cause disengagement, which future research should test.

Could it be task switching? Yes, this is a plausible alternative. In the photo conditions participants had to switch from one task (operating the phone: framing, taking, deleting, pressing the spacebar) to another (studying the painting). Task switching carries switch costs: time and control are needed to reconfigure for the new task, and attention may remain partly on the previous task (attention residue). This could reduce encoding at the start of the 15 s. A problem for this account is that classic switch costs last only a short time, while viewing lasted 15 s; still, attention residue could last longer, and the authors themselves admit that any secondary task might produce the effect.

How to test it. Add a condition with a secondary task that also requires switching but involves no photo (e.g., typing the painting’s title on the phone, or a tone-counting task) of the same duration. If memory is impaired as much as in the Delete condition, a general task-switching/secondary-task account is supported; if photo-taking impairs memory more, there is something specific about photographing (such as the metacognitive illusion).

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸Impairment continues after the camera is put down
  • ▸Authors: disengagement via metacognitive illusion or automatic offloading
  • ▸Alternative: task-switch cost / attention residue
  • ▸Authors admit any secondary task might do it
  • ▸Test: non-photo secondary task of equal duration
The Delete finding rules out time but not task: it shows the cost is in what the photo does to the mind, not in how long you look.
🪝 Memory hook: After answering a text, you ‘look’ at the lecture slide again, but your mind is still half on the phone.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Only repeating ‘attentional disengagement’ without the mechanisms.
  • Answering yes/no to task switching without explaining or testing it.
  • Forgetting that viewing time was equal (or longer).
Question C6

Why would it be incorrect to conclude on the basis of this study that taking pictures creates less memorable experiences?

🧭 What the question asks: Show the gap between what was measured and the broad claim. Name concrete limits of the DV, the task, the sample and the photo situation.

✍️ Answer

The conclusion goes far beyond the data, for several reasons:

  • Narrow DV. The study measured recognition of visual details of paintings on a multiple-choice test. A ‘memorable experience’ also includes gist, emotions, enjoyment, meaning and the social context, none of which were measured.
  • Short retention interval, no photo review. Memory was tested after 10 minutes, without access to the photos. In real life photos can act as powerful retrieval cues later (SenseCam: Berry et al., 2007; Loveday & Conway, 2011), so photographed experiences may be remembered better in the long run, provided people actually look at their photos.
  • Instructed, not volitional photos. Participants were told what to photograph. When people choose what to photograph, it can increase engagement and memory for visual aspects (Diehl, Zauberman & Barasch, 2016; Barasch et al., 2017), and automatic wearable cameras had no effect (Niforatos et al., 2017).
  • Artificial experience. Paintings on a computer screen in a lab are not a holiday, a concert or a wedding; ecological validity is limited.
  • Sample. Small groups of UCSC undergraduates participating for course credit.
  • Relative, not absolute. The finding is that photographed paintings were remembered less than observed ones, not that the experience was not memorable.

So the correct conclusion is narrower: under these lab conditions, being instructed to take a photo reduces short-term memory for visual details of the photographed object.

🖼️ The answer in one picture

📌 Key points

  • ▸DV = visual details only, not the experience
  • ▸10-min delay; photos never reviewed
  • ▸Instructed vs volitional photos (Barasch et al., 2017)
  • ▸Lab paintings, student sample
  • ▸Relative impairment, not ‘unmemorable’
Always match the claim to the measure: ‘less memory for visual details after 10 minutes’ is not ‘less memorable experiences’.
🪝 Memory hook: Measuring one ingredient and judging the whole meal.
⚠️ Where marks are lost
  • Only saying ‘small sample’.
  • Missing the volitional-photography evidence.
  • Forgetting that photos can help later as retrieval cues.

📋 One-line answers

QuestionOne-line answer
B1 VideoNew episodes lost within minutes, repetition, disorientation; STM, intelligence, old memories and skills spared.
B2 Problem 2Dissociations between STM and LTM (HM vs KF; recency vs primacy) and between working-memory subsystems.
B3 Huppert & PiercyPatients use familiarity instead of context, so repeated day-1 items feel recent: item–context binding fails.
B4 Remember/know3A: childhood amnesia (Multhaup et al., 2005): ‘know’ → ‘remember’ at ~4.7 years.
B5 ScreeningTests in the delay interfere with fragile consolidation (Dewar et al., 2010), so recall is underestimated.
C1 ArticleOne within-subjects IV (3 levels); DV visual-detail MC; Observe best; significant, d 0.5–1.2; generalisation limited.
C2 ExamplesPeople: family, team, friends. Devices: contacts, calendar, search engine, navigation.
C3 Offloading figureSnapchat/Delete would rise to Observe level; only Camera low. Not what happened.
C4 Best designExperiment 2: equal viewing time, believable deletion, power analysis.
C5 Delete resultAuthors: continued disengagement (metacognitive illusion, automatic offloading). Task switching is a plausible alternative.

Putting A, B and C together

🧵 Synthesis

One thread links B and C: memory depends on binding an experience to its context, and anything that disrupts that binding costs memory. In amnesia, the hippocampal ‘glue’ is damaged, so patients keep items and skills but lose the where and when (B1, B3), rely on familiarity instead of recollection (B4), and lose fragile new traces to interference (B5). In healthy people, photo-taking may disrupt the same encoding of the experience, not because the camera stores it for us, but because our attention and effort drop (C3, C5).

Exam tip: the tutorial also trains research thinking: dissociations as evidence for separate systems (B2), crossover patterns as stronger evidence than simple deficits (B3), measurement effects (B5), deriving predictions from theories (C3) and matching claims to measures (C6).
